body:
I just profiled both current and your suggestion, I couldn't detect much performance difference (at most 1 usec improvement). That's around going through 5-8 actions. With the counter, you do have to go through all actions. But when you detect if the action is pressed, you can just exit the loop with `return` immediately. Most of the time the user would actually be pressing something, so we're interested in short-cutting I think. If the user is away, the performance doesn't matter anyway. So, readability would be preferred in this case imo.

I'll try to see if there's any more significant difference with more actions, but I doubt the user would like to define many of them. Maybe:
```
"Invalid operands for bit shifting. Only positive operands are supported, and the right hand side operand cannot be higher than 62."
```

That being said, I don't think if it's worth it to limit to `b <= 62`.
It will still wrap around if you do `2 << 62` with a signed int, or `4 << 62` with an unsigned it. Only `1 << 62` would be safe.

IMO a note in the documentation should be sufficient to make users aware that bitshifting can lead to wrapping around if they exceed the number of bits of the used type. Maybe we can have some GDScript warnings for that eventually too, but I wouldn't prevent the operation if we can't guarantee that we handle all cases.

So I'd suggest leaving it to only signessness checks, and the error:
```
Invalid operands for bit shifting. Only positive operands are supported.
```

The work overall looks really good, and it's going to be a great improvement.

Some things worries me though:

1. This will break workflow for people who uses different scripts for client and server. Unless the script have the same exposed RPC/RSET (order shouldn't matter since sorting is done based on case). This is okay in general, but it needs to fail properly. Maybe we can spend a byte to do a checksum (xors of function names/...) so it's detectable and we can report it.

2. As pointed out in comments, if I understood correctly the code, exposing a new method via rpc_config will just append it. This means that different rpc_config order will result in differnt ids being assigned, and the wrong function to be called. Shouldn't we re-sort them when that happens? That will fix that problem, but ongoing calls with that ID will fail instead. For now, `rpc_config` seems to crash the engine when the new RPC is sent (see attached code).

3. The encoding optimization should probably be moved to marshalls, but I guess that could be done in a later PR.

Of all the points, `2` worries me the most. I feel we have to find a solution to that. Do you have anything in mind (maybe some form of versioning?). Using an agreed upon ID like we do for paths is less optimized and it would be a pity to waste the work done so far on generating the ID.

body:
In C++, memory allocated with `new` must be freed with `delete` and memory allocated with `alloc` must use `free`. Depending on the implementation `new` and `alloc` can track allocated memory separately (https://isocpp.org/wiki/faq/freestore-mgmt#mixing-malloc-and-delete), and `free` won't call object destructor.

With current Godot memory management implementation and no destructor in the `screensaver`, `memfree` might work, but it is wrong anyway.

I am against delta ever being allowed to be zero or negative.

Everyone expects delta to be change-in-time-since-last-process. It is physically impossible for a perfectly accurate timer to say no time has passed, as calling functions **always** takes time. So yes, it is physically possible to get a measurement of zero for the passed time since the last frame, however improbable that is. body:
I don't see what all the fuss is. No gain will come from receiving a time based event with no time having passed. I for one cannot believe that this simple thing is so debated and left this way.

I have written toy engines myself in C and GL and have had to fix jitter and the like, and none of it was ever because no time passed between frames. This sounds 100% like covering up the real problem: Bad time source.

On Win32, QueryPerformanceCounter provides for nanosecond accuracy on most hardware that I tested. This guarantees that the second query will be after the first, and there's no way that, given the amount of work Godot must do, for a delta of 0 or less to EVER appear. Delta is simply current_frame_time - last_frame_time. If there's jitter, keep 7 of the last deltas, sort them, toss 0 and 6, 1,2,3,4,5 average, and give that value to process functions. I don't get why there's anything more needed.

Even if a zero time did appear, you're doing work based on time. Whatever that work is, you'd do none of it if delta was zero. Wasted cycles, wasted energy. Just throw out the process event if <= 0, seriously. It's not like anything is going to break... no time passed, remember? And the next tiny slice of time will get the process call, so again... no problems, but it's fixed. No potential gachas for newbies who (imo correctly) assume that time always marches forward. No chance of causing any issues because of a dropped _process, because it'll happen again *extremely* soon.

If I'm missing some key piece to this that would make this a no-go, please do clue me in.

body:
You are 100% correct: All of this IS a way to compensate for a bad timer source. The problem isn't the timer resolution, though, it's that the time is taken on the CPU. In the best case (single threaded operation), when all the commands have been passed to the GPU. In the worst case (multithread), when all the scene data has been passed to the rendering thread. If you want stable frame time measurements, you should take the time when the GPU is starting to deliver the newly rendered frame to the screen. Alas, in GLES, that seems to be impossible. In Desktop OpenGL and Vulkan, you can use fences and queries to determine when the GPU flipped the buffers N frames ago. It's a bit difficult because it's asynchronous, but doable. Patches probably welcome.

The entire purpose of the file that is getting patched here is to take the imperfect timer measurements and derive stable process calls. Focus is on getting consistent number of physics steps per render frame. Without the code in this file, Godot would sometimes, even in perfect 60FPS VSync locked conditions, do jittery updates where each frame, anything between 0 and 2 physics updates were performed, because the imperfect timer measurements would lie just a little bit on either side of a threshold. Averaging over N frames makes these occurrences rarer, but does not fix them.

The negative timesteps that are corrected in this patch aren't coming from the timer itself, they're a bad output of the correction. Essentially, it's overshooting a bit one frame, then tries to backpedal. Maybe it would be possible to just prevent the overshooting; I don't think so, because that's what the system has to do to function correctly when frame times decrease. I opted for the post-correction also because that guarantees there are no side effects, it's easier to prove that the result will be correct, and it'll stay correct even if the core gets changed.

Just not calling _process() if the argument would be 0 is also not such a good option. There are three possible expectations here:
1. The sum of delta arguments to _process() is as close to the total program runtime as possible. Networked games rely on that.
2. the argument to _process() should be positive. That is what you want, even though it was never really guaranteed (just extremely unlikely to be false).
3. _process is called for every rendered frame. That is [documented](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/getting_started/step_by_step/scripting_continued.html?highlight=_process#processing).
Best possible conformance with expectation 1, in the situation covered here, requires to either violate 2 or 3. You get screamed at by someone no matter what :)

The current, updated patch opts to violate expectation 1 a little to save 2 and 3. But not more than it is allowed to; the limit on real time/game time deviation still is less than physics_jitter_fix/physics_fps. I personally would prefer to break bad client code, but do so early; I don't really see a way to do that well, though, and don't want that to be the hill this bugfix dies on.

body:
@Shatur95 The reason we only plan on allowing a subset of modern C++ is to ease online code reviews (among other things). When you're a pull request reviewer, you typically don't clone people's branches in an IDE; you just rely on GitHub's code viewer which doesn't provide things like type information on hover. For instance, this is why we'll disallow the use of `auto` in Godot's codebase.

Unlike `auto`, `constexpr` doesn't suffer from readability issues, but I remember seeing reduz being opposed to it (I don't know why).
